metadata.title: Moncton City Council Performance Scorecards
metadata.author: Ward 2 resident
metadata.methodology: This evaluation framework was developed independently of any individual councillor and is designed to be applied to any member of Moncton City Council. Sources include CBC News reporting, Radio-Canada, 91.9 The Bend, Acadie Nouvelle, City of Moncton official documents and meeting minutes, and council meeting records available through the city. All six categories are weighted equally. The author is a Ward 2 resident.

councillors.term_info: 2021–2025 · Re-elected 2021 unopposed · Appointed to the Senate of Canada on March 7, 2025

councillors.overall_assessment:
Dawn Arnold presided over the most consequential period in modern Moncton history. The city grew faster than almost anywhere else in Canada during her tenure — a 5.1% population increase from 2023 to 2024 that ranked second nationally — and her administration positioned Moncton to absorb that growth with major investments in housing, infrastructure, and climate planning. The $36.3 million downtown infrastructure overhaul, the $15.5 million Housing Accelerator Fund, the net-zero emissions plan, and the 25-year Urban Growth Strategy are all tangible deliverables from her time in office.

Her personal conduct was professional throughout and free of code of conduct complaints. When decisions went wrong — most visibly the closed-door menorah vote — she issued a public acknowledgment and reversed course. The willingness to own a mistake at the height of national media attention is a meaningful test of character, and she passed it.

The main weaknesses are institutional rather than personal. Private meeting practices did not meet provincial legislated requirements — a gap discovered in a December 2025 review and a notable oversight for an administration that publicly championed transparency. The city did not systematically track the number of in-camera sessions. And the RCMP decision in February 2024 — one of the most consequential policing choices in the city's recent history — proceeded without public consultation despite requests from five councillors. These are governance gaps that fell within the mayor's sphere of responsibility to fix.

Her appointment to the Senate of Canada in March 2025 cut short her second term but speaks to her stature in federal circles. The central question for her legacy is whether the remarkable growth Moncton achieved was well-governed growth — and the honest answer is mostly yes, with meaningful blind spots in oversight and public engagement that will be left for her successor to address.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No code of conduct violations were filed against Mayor Arnold during either of her terms, and she carried herself with the composure and discipline the office demands. Her handling of the menorah controversy in late 2023 is the clearest test of her professional conduct under pressure. When council's closed-door unanimous vote to remove religious symbols from City Hall drew national attention and a petition with over 6,000 signatures, Arnold did not deflect or minimize. She issued a public statement within days acknowledging the city had "acted too quickly," appeared before media, and led the reversal.

She also handled the two Bourgeois code of conduct investigations with appropriate gravity, stating the matter was being taken "very seriously" when the 2021 complaint was launched against her council colleague — a position that acknowledged the severity of the allegations without prejudging the outcome.

The one concern is procedural: the menorah decision itself was made in a closed session without public consultation, on a matter with obvious and predictable religious and cultural sensitivities. A more cautious judgment call at the front end would have been preferable to a principled reversal at the back end. That said, the reversal itself — transparent, prompt, and public — is the more memorable data point.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.note: UPDATED: Revised from B- based on documented Facebook posts showing detailed post-meeting summaries after every council meeting.
categories.assessment:
Arnold maintained a consistent practice of posting detailed, bilingual summaries after every council meeting on social media — specific dollar figures, agenda items, and an open invitation for constituent questions. This level of proactive communication is not the norm for elected officials at any level, and it represents genuine commitment to keeping residents informed in a direct, accessible way that bypasses institutional gatekeeping.

The city also posted dates and topics of private meetings during her tenure, and council meeting materials were publicly available. She supported open data initiatives and the city's publicly accessible budget information portal.

However, a 2024 CBC investigation found the city does not track the number of in-camera sessions at all — creating a gap between the claim that private meetings are kept to an "absolute minimum" and any ability to verify that claim. In 2019, Arnold floated the idea of investigating a leak after CBC published information from a confidential council meeting, raising questions about her instincts when institutional confidentiality and press freedom collide. Most significantly, a December 2025 review found the city's private meetings bylaw did not meet provincial requirements — a systemic governance failure that persisted through her entire second term. The grade recognizes Arnold's genuine personal transparency while acknowledging these institutional gaps.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
This is Arnold's strongest category and it is not particularly close. Her administration delivered on multiple policy fronts simultaneously during a period of extraordinary demand on city services.

The $36.3 million joint federal-provincial-municipal downtown infrastructure investment included the complete overhaul of Downing Street and surrounding blocks — a project that had been deferred for years. The Community Energy and Emissions Plan committed the city to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 with 31 concrete action steps, not just an aspirational target. The 25-year Urban Growth Strategy, released in 2024, established a long-range planning framework the city had previously lacked.

On housing, her administration secured $15.5 million through the federal Housing Accelerator Fund, committed $6 million to Rising Tide Community Initiatives for supportive housing, launched the Downtown Densification Grant Program, and pushed council to approve 4-unit housing across all residential zones — a significant zoning shift that unlocked federal infrastructure funding and brought the city in line with national housing reform priorities.

The economic results during her tenure were striking: second-highest population growth rate in Canada, building permits up 50% year-over-year in Q2 2024, multiple consecutive years of residential tax rate cuts while expanding services. The CUPE Local 51 collective bargaining agreement was concluded without a labour disruption and described as genuinely collaborative by both parties.

The caveat is attribution: Moncton's growth was driven by powerful demographic and economic forces — Atlantic immigration policy, interprovincial migration, relative housing affordability — that no mayor creates or controls. But effective leadership means positioning a city to capitalize on opportunity when it arrives, and Arnold's administration demonstrably did that.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
Arnold's most successful collaboration was intergovernmental: coordinating federal, provincial, and municipal partnerships on infrastructure, housing, and immigration required sustained relationship management with multiple levels of government, and the results — $36.3M infrastructure, $15.5M housing, federal housing reform alignment — show this was done effectively.

Within council, the picture is more complicated. Council adopted a public values statement committing to integrity, honesty, and inclusion — a signal of collaborative intent at the leadership level. The CUPE agreement demonstrated productive labour relations. But the RCMP decision in February 2024 produced a 6-5 split that exposed a divided council, with Arnold voting alongside the majority to proceed without public consultation over the objections of five colleagues. Whether that outcome reflects a failure of consensus-building or simply an intractable disagreement is a matter of interpretation, but the result was a contentious vote on the most consequential policing decision of the term.

The menorah incident — made in closed session, then reversed under pressure — also reflects a moment where stronger early consultation with colleagues and community would have prevented a damaging national story.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
Arnold championed Moncton's identity as Canada's first officially bilingual city and positioned newcomer integration as a civic priority at exactly the moment it mattered most. With 46% of New Brunswick's permanent resident admissions choosing Greater Moncton in 2024, her consistent messaging that "newcomers have been, and continue to be, a vital part of Greater Moncton's growth story" was substantively accurate and politically courageous at a time when immigration has become a contested issue in many communities.

Her administration engaged the public on the Climate Change Adaptation Plan, the Green Development Guidelines, and the Urban Growth Strategy — all policy areas where early community input shaped the final product. The 6,000-signature petition that prompted the menorah reversal demonstrates both the depth of community feeling on cultural and religious inclusion, and Arnold's responsiveness to that sentiment when it was clearly expressed.

The main limitation is the RCMP decision, where Arnold's majority voted down a proposal for public consultation on a question — the future of the city's policing model — that directly affects every resident. For a mayor who built her brand on civic engagement and bilingual inclusion, declining to bring the community into a major policing decision is a notable inconsistency.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
Arnold's financial management was solid. Four consecutive years of residential tax rate cuts while growing services is a meaningful fiscal achievement in a period of inflationary pressure. Annual external audits by KPMG provided independent financial oversight. The 2025 budget of $223.8 million operating, with 38 new positions, reflected managed growth rather than unconstrained expansion. Council voted down a proposed 34.2% salary increase formula in 2022, demonstrating fiscal discipline on a politically awkward question.

However, the institutional oversight record has real gaps. The absence of systematic tracking of in-camera sessions means there is no verifiable baseline for the "absolute minimum" claim about private meetings. The code of conduct bylaw was found to not meet provincial legislative requirements in a 2025 review — a failure of legal compliance that persisted undetected through her entire second term. There is no documented evidence of independent performance audits for major capital investments like the Avenir Centre or the downtown densification program. And the RCMP decision proceeded without the full data analysis that Butler and others requested, on a $57 million infrastructure question. These are not minor process gaps — they represent the kind of institutional oversight that prevents compounding governance failures, and they fall within the mayor's responsibility to address.

councillors.overall_assessment:
Dave Steeves had a solid first term with one defining episode: the religious symbols reversal in December 2023. When a closed-door council vote to remove a menorah and nativity scene from City Hall drew national criticism and a 6,000-person petition, Steeves — alongside Butler and Crossman, who had all voted against the removal in the private session — introduced the motion to reverse course and argued publicly that decisions of this nature should be made in public. The reversal was unanimous. The honest reading is that the public response made reversal inevitable; the credit Steeves deserves is for being on the right side before it was the obvious side, and for stepping forward to formalize it.

Beyond that defining moment, Steeves operated as a responsive, community-connected first-term councillor who engaged seriously with Ward 3 constituents on traffic safety, environmental quality, and community infrastructure. His clean conduct record and the respect he earned from colleagues — evidenced by Butler's nomination of him for Deputy Mayor in 2024 — suggest a councillor with genuine professional integrity.

The limitations are common to first-term councillors: a reactive policy posture, limited depth of budget scrutiny, and deference to institutional processes rather than challenging them. His vote for the Elmwood Drive subdivisions against staff advice and planning committee recommendations raises questions about whether constituent pressure sometimes outweighs expert planning guidance in his decision-making framework. These are areas to watch as he potentially enters a second term.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No code of conduct violations or complaints were found against Steeves during this term. He received the Queen Elizabeth II Platinum Jubilee Medal in 2022 for extraordinary community contribution — a recognition that speaks to his standing beyond the council chamber.

His background as Associate Pastor of Family Ministries at Hillside Church and Executive Director of the Buckingham Leadership Institute provides a professional foundation in community leadership. He holds a Master's in Leadership from Liberty University and a Bachelor of Kinesiology from UNB. These academic and professional credentials are consistent with his measured, constructive demeanour in council proceedings.

Of all eleven members evaluated on this council, Steeves has the cleanest conduct record. In a term marked by two formal code of conduct violations involving another councillor, and considerable interpersonal friction during divisive debates, his ability to maintain professionalism while still advocating firmly for his positions is worth noting explicitly.

A planning committee appointment episode is the most significant blemish on Steeves's conduct record. According to a credible account from a sitting councillor, Steeves voted with the majority to reject the entire slate of Municipal Plan Review Committee candidates at the August 19, 2024 meeting — a vote that had the clear effect of blocking a vetted community activist from the committee despite her having been recommended by city staff. Unlike several colleagues, Steeves did not document his opposition in writing, and his name does not appear in the emails obtained by Brunswick News. But a vote is a vote. Using a committee appointment process to exclude a citizen on the basis of her public criticism of council is incompatible with the A- grade this category previously carried.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
The religious symbols episode is Steeves's most significant transparency moment — and the full picture reflects better on him than the initial headlines suggested. Steeves voted against the motion to remove the menorah and nativity scene in the private December 2023 session, a position he disclosed publicly on Facebook that same weekend before the reversal vote. He then introduced the motion to reverse the decision and explicitly argued that decisions of this nature should be made openly. That combination — dissenting privately, disclosing publicly, and leading the corrective action — reflects a principled transparency position rather than a purely pragmatic response to pressure. He was on the right side of this file before the backlash, not just because of it.

He engages with media and constituents on local issues, publicly voices his positions on traffic safety and noise concerns, and his voting record is documented through council minutes. He supported the investigation into the north end odour issue, which itself is a form of accountability for a persistent quality-of-life concern.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
For a first-term councillor, Steeves has been meaningfully active without being transformative. The religious symbols episode is the clearest moment of principled action in Steeves's term. He voted against the removal in the private session, publicly disclosed his position before the reversal, and introduced the motion to reinstate the displays. The credit is real — but it belongs to his private vote and his willingness to step forward, not to political manoeuvring. The reversal was driven by public demand: a 6,000-person petition and national media attention left council little choice. Steeves formalized an inevitable outcome and framed it well.

He supported the Harvest House grant increase from $57,500 to $100,000, citing the concrete value of the organization's work rather than general support for social services. He engaged on the north end odour issue by supporting a task force and consultant review that eventually traced the source to a sewage composting facility — a case where constituent advocacy led to a documented investigation and finding. He has been vocal and consistent on traffic safety in Ward 3, raising the issue repeatedly and connecting it to specific constituent experiences including a child struck while cycling.

The mixed results include his vote for the Elmwood Drive subdivisions despite staff opposition and planning committee recommendations against them. While individual planning votes are judgment calls, overriding expert advice on anti-sprawl policy has long-term fiscal implications — infrastructure servicing costs for low-density subdivisions are a well-documented municipal budget challenge. His ongoing traffic safety concerns remain largely unresolved.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
The religious symbols episode reflects well on Steeves, but the credit belongs more to his principled private vote than to any act of coalition-building. He, Butler, and Crossman had all voted against the removal in the closed session. When the public response — a 6,000-person petition and national media coverage — made the reversal inevitable, Steeves stepped forward to introduce the motion and frame it publicly as a transparency issue. That framing was valuable. But the colleagues who reversed did so because of public pressure, not because they were persuaded. The unanimous result was a product of the moment, not a measure of persuasive skill.

His working relationship with fellow Ward 3 councillor Bryan Butler is productive — they collaborate on shared ward issues and Butler nominated him for Deputy Mayor in May 2024, indicating genuine peer respect. He participates constructively in council debates across a range of issues and his occasional minority positions (such as on the House of Nazareth retroactive grant) appear to be principled disagreements rather than a pattern of isolation.

For a first-term councillor learning the dynamics of a divided council, Steeves's collaborative track record is above average. He has not accumulated the interpersonal friction that limits some colleagues, and he has demonstrated the persuasive capacity that marks effective legislators.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
Steeves maintains an active social media presence with regular constituent updates and demonstrates consistent responsiveness to community concerns in Ward 3's north end. His engagement on the odour issue, traffic safety, and noise concerns shows he listens to constituents and brings their concerns into council deliberations with specific, documented examples rather than general advocacy.

His background in ministry and community leadership gives him natural constituent-facing skills — the ability to listen carefully, make people feel heard, and translate personal concerns into institutional language. His response to the child cycling incident in Ward 3 illustrated this: he connected a specific community experience directly to a policy request for traffic-calming infrastructure.

The limitation is proactive outreach. Steeves's engagement model appears primarily responsive — residents bring problems to him and he acts on them — rather than proactively seeking input on ward development priorities or hosting structured community events. The strongest community engagement combines responsiveness with proactive consultation, and the latter is less visible in his record.

A planning committee appointment episode introduces a meaningful qualification to Steeves's engagement record. Voting to block a vetted community activist from participating in the Municipal Plan Review Committee — a document meant to guide Moncton's growth for the next decade — because of her public criticism of council is a failure of community representation. Engaged citizens who challenge council decisions are precisely the voices a municipal plan review process should include, not exclude. This note is based on a credible account from a sitting councillor; Steeves does not appear in the documentary email record published by Brunswick News.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
Steeves's oversight record is uneven. His challenge to the religious symbols decision-making process reflects institutional scrutiny in the broad sense — questioning whether a closed-door process was appropriate for a culturally significant decision. His support for the north end odour task force kept pressure on a slow-moving environmental investigation.

However, he voted with the majority to keep the RCMP and to reject a proposal for public consultation before finalizing the decision — opposing the additional scrutiny that five colleagues believed was warranted on a $57M infrastructure commitment. He voted for the Elmwood Drive subdivisions against staff recommendations and planning committee opposition, overriding expert advice on a planning matter.

There is limited evidence of Steeves engaging in detailed budget scrutiny, requesting additional staff reports, or challenging financial assumptions in committee. This is not unusual for first-term councillors who are still building domain expertise, but the strongest performers establish a scrutiny presence early.

councillors.overall_assessment:
Charles Léger is a policy-oriented, third-term councillor who has carved out a distinctive niche in public safety, progressive social policy, and housing. His guaranteed livable basic income motion — passed unanimously in September 2022 — demonstrates a rare ability on a divided council: championing a bold idea in a way that brings every colleague along. Getting a unanimous vote on anything is an achievement in municipal politics; getting one on a progressive social policy proposal is more remarkable still.

His focus on downtown crime, abandoned housing, and housing density reflects genuine responsiveness to the most pressing concerns of Ward 2 and central Moncton more broadly. His business background — an MBA and 30+ years in the private sector — gives him a credibility on fiscal matters that complements rather than conflicts with his social policy instincts.

The main limitations are depth of follow-through and breadth of oversight. Short-term rental regulation remains pending despite years of advocacy. Abandoned housing remains a persistent problem in Ward 2. Downtown crime has not been resolved by the security patrol pilot. These are systemic challenges that no single councillor controls, but the gap between Léger's advocacy and documented outcomes is real. His mayoral candidacy for 2026 will be a test of whether his policy vision can scale from Ward 2 to city-wide leadership.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No code of conduct violations were found in Léger's public record during this term. His appointment as Deputy Mayor in June 2021 — by his council peers — indicates the professional confidence colleagues place in him, a meaningful signal on a council that experienced significant interpersonal conflict during the same period.

His MBA and 30+ years in the private sector provide a professional foundation, and his presidency of the Friends of the Cathedral — an active heritage preservation organization — demonstrates constructive community leadership outside the council chamber. His demeanour in council proceedings is professional and measured, with none of the confrontational edge that generated formal complaints for at least one colleague.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
Léger has demonstrated transparency in specific, documented ways. He moved a motion for dedicated downtown security patrols with clear public articulation of the rationale and funding requirements. He called for special council meetings to address public safety concerns in June 2022, creating a public forum for an issue constituents were raising privately. He pushed for short-term rental safety regulations with an explicit public case connecting Moncton's regulatory gap to the deadly Montreal apartment fire of April 2023.

However, his transparency profile is largely reactive and issue-specific rather than systemic. He does not appear to have publicly challenged the closed-door process for the RCMP decision, even while voting against its outcome. There is limited evidence of proactive transparency initiatives — regular constituent reporting, open budget briefings, or public explanations of votes on non-headline issues.

His overall transparency record is adequate but inconsistent — strong when he has a specific policy argument to make, and less visible when the institutional process itself is the issue.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
Léger's most notable initiative was the guaranteed livable basic income motion in September 2022, co-introduced with Councillor Thériault. The motion passed unanimously — a result that requires both policy vision and the political skill to build consensus across a divided table. For a municipal council to take a formal position on a federal-provincial social policy question requires a councillor willing to lead on an issue that sits outside the conventional scope of city government, and Léger was that councillor.

His downtown security initiative led to a $288,000 pilot project with RCMP visibility patrols operational by March 2025 — a concrete outcome from a sustained advocacy campaign. He pushed for enforcement timelines on abandoned housing, a persistent Ward 2 quality-of-life issue that had previously drifted without resolution. He championed the 4-unit housing zoning change that council approved in April 2025, a significant land-use reform that unlocked $15.5M in federal infrastructure funding and represented real progress on housing density.

The caveat is that several of Léger's signature advocacy campaigns have produced limited concrete resolution. Short-term rental regulation was still pending as of 2025 despite his advocacy since 2023. Abandoned housing remains a recurring complaint in Ward 2. The downtown security patrol pilot addressed symptoms without resolving root causes. These outcomes reflect systemic limits more than personal failures, but they temper the overall effectiveness grade.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
The basic income motion — securing unanimous support on an ambitious progressive proposal — is Léger's strongest evidence of coalition-building. His appointment as Deputy Mayor in 2021 also reflects broad peer confidence. He worked constructively with Thériault on the basic income motion and served on multiple committees including crime reduction and planning advisory.

On the term's defining vote — the RCMP decision — Léger was part of the five-member minority, placing him in direct opposition to the mayor and a narrow majority on the most consequential policing decision in recent Moncton history. While his position had principled merit, being on the losing side of a close vote on a major issue creates relationship friction that limited what he could accomplish through collaboration in subsequent months.

His collaboration profile is strongest on issues he initiates or co-initiates, and less visible when navigating disagreements initiated by others.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
Léger has been engaged with downtown and West End Ward 2 constituents on the issues that matter most to them. He responded to complaints about cannabis odour from Organigram, advocated for enforcement on abandoned properties in response to constituent frustration, and called for special council meetings specifically because of community-raised safety concerns. He maintains an active Facebook presence and engages consistently with local media on ward issues.

His heritage preservation work through the Friends of the Cathedral adds a cultural dimension to his community engagement — it demonstrates investment in Moncton's built environment that extends beyond the legislative agenda.

The gap is systematic, proactive engagement beyond the crime and safety file. There is no evidence of structured ward consultations, town halls, or proactive outreach on housing density, transportation, or services. Léger appears primarily reactive in his community engagement — deeply responsive to the issues constituents raise, but less visible in proactively shaping the agenda or soliciting input on future-oriented decisions.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
Léger has shown oversight instincts on specific, important files. Calling for special council meetings to debate public safety is a scrutiny function — it forces institutional engagement with issues that might otherwise be deferred. His May 2025 demand for KPIs and evidence of crime reduction before approving additional RCMP hiring is precisely the kind of evidence-based oversight that distinguishes good council watchdogs from passive approvers. His advocacy for timeline enforcement on abandoned houses exercises the city's regulatory authority in a way that holds property owners accountable.

His opposition to the RCMP decision, and his advocacy for a longer, more data-driven process, represents substantive institutional scrutiny on a major expenditure decision.

The limitation is depth and consistency. There are no documented instances of Léger challenging budget line items comprehensively, requesting independent reviews of department spending, or conducting the kind of granular financial scrutiny that would characterize the strongest oversight performers. His scrutiny is concentrated on the issues he cares most about — policing and safety — and less visible across the full range of municipal operations.

councillors.overall_assessment:
Bryan Butler brings 34 years of law enforcement experience — with the Moncton Police Force and the RCMP — to a council role that frequently grapples with policing questions. That expertise is genuine and it shows: his contributions to the RCMP service review were substantive, his town halls on north end community safety drew over 100 residents, and his ability to explain the mechanics of policing deployment to neighbours is a form of public education that most councillors cannot provide.

His community engagement through Ward 3 town halls and his long-standing advocacy on flooding and community infrastructure show a councillor who maintains direct constituent contact beyond the council chamber. His gracious public response to losing the RCMP vote — "that's democracy, and I'm happy with that" — reflects the kind of democratic maturity that public life requires.

The main concerns are a pattern of stepping back from institutional challenges rather than working through them (the Social Inclusion Committee resignation being the clearest example) and a contradictory approach to accountability (championing transparency on specific decisions while opposing the independent oversight mechanism that would deliver it systematically). Butler is a stronger ward councillor than he is a city-wide institutional force.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No code of conduct violations were found against Butler during this term. His 34 years in law enforcement — Moncton Police Force from 1979 to 1988, RCMP from 1988 to 2013 — provide a professional foundation that is visible in his structured, evidence-oriented approach to council debates on policing and public safety. His Queen's Diamond Jubilee Medal (2012) recognizes community contribution during his law enforcement career.

His election as Deputy Mayor in May 2022, even amid process concerns that prompted Mayor Arnold to acknowledge the selection mechanism made "many around the table feel uncomfortable," resulted in a 7-4 majority — indicating genuine peer support despite the procedural awkwardness. His conduct during that period was not at issue.

His 2019 vote against hiring an integrity commissioner — the institutional mechanism for independent oversight of council conduct — is the one conduct-adjacent concern. For a former law enforcement officer who built a career around institutional accountability frameworks, opposing an accountability body for elected officials reflects an inconsistency that limits this grade.

On the religious symbols file, Butler publicly stated he voted against the motion to remove the menorah and nativity scene in the private session — placing him on the principled side of that decision before the public backlash made reversal inevitable. It is a genuine positive in an otherwise mixed conduct record.

A planning committee appointment episode is a serious conduct failure that significantly undermines this category. Butler was one of five councillors who put his opposition to the appointment in writing, emailing: 'She has been very disrespectful towards members of council. Not just on this matter but many decisions we have made. I also have no problem stating this in open council.' He then voted to reject the entire slate of staff-recommended candidates at the August 19 meeting, helping stall a provincially mandated committee. His public justification afterward — that council wanted members 'on the same wavelength' — was among the most candid and damaging statements of the episode. Treating public criticism of council as a disqualifier for volunteer civic work is a meaningful departure from the professional standards a councillor should uphold.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
Butler's strongest transparency moment was his handling of the RCMP vote outcome. He publicly stated "we have to give answers to the public" before the vote, advocated for extending the decision timeline to gather more data and analysis, and after losing the 6-5 vote, defended his dissenting position publicly and gracefully: "that's democracy, and I'm happy with that." The combination of pre-vote advocacy for more public information and post-vote acceptance of the democratic outcome is a model of accountable conduct.

However, his 2019 vote against an integrity commissioner creates a significant tension. He argued the position would "only make recommendations" with enforcement returning to council — a technically accurate description that understates the considerable value of independent investigation, public reporting, and the deterrent effect of third-party scrutiny. Championing transparency on individual decisions while opposing the institutional infrastructure that delivers it systematically is a genuine inconsistency, not a minor footnote.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
Butler served as Deputy Mayor from May 2022 to May 2023 and co-chaired the Social Inclusion Committee with Councillor Paul Pellerin — two roles that placed him in positions of leadership on the city's most pressing social challenges. The Social Inclusion Committee resignation is the defining failure in this category. He stepped back from a committee responsible for affordable housing and homelessness policy during the period when Moncton's homelessness crisis was at its most acute, citing "increased workload" and frustration that "we were spinning our wheels waiting for the money, but the money never came."

The frustration is understandable — waiting for senior government funding that doesn't materialize is genuinely difficult. But the strongest committee chairs push through institutional obstacles rather than stepping aside, and the timing — mid-crisis — makes the departure particularly notable.

His Ward 3 advocacy on flooding and the North End Community Centre shows sustained constituency-level commitment. His law enforcement background provided unique perspective on policing decisions. But the absence of major, independently-initiated city-wide projects limits the overall grade.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
Butler shows genuine collaborative instincts in the right contexts. Co-chairing the Social Inclusion Committee, organizing joint town halls with Ward 3 colleague Dave Steeves, and nominating Steeves for Deputy Mayor in 2024 all reflect constructive relationship-building within his ward. His Deputy Mayor election — despite the process concerns — secured a 7-4 majority, indicating broad council support.

His response to the RCMP vote outcome was notably collaborative in spirit: accepting the democratic result gracefully and committing to work within the majority's framework. That kind of cooperative acceptance of defeat is not universal on divided councils and is worth acknowledging.

The RCMP vote placed him in a five-person minority that failed to secure a sixth vote on the term's most significant policing decision — a result that suggests the cross-council coalition work needed to influence major outcomes fell short. And the Social Inclusion Committee resignation removed him from a collaborative institutional role at a critical moment.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
This is Butler's strongest area. The public town halls on community safety in Ward 3's north end — drawing over 100 residents in 2024 — represent the kind of face-to-face constituent engagement that translates directly into accountability and representation. Residents who attend a town hall where their councillor explains policing deployment options, listens to their concerns, and commits to follow-up are receiving a qualitatively different form of representation than residents who receive a form letter.

His law enforcement background creates credibility with constituents on safety issues — he can explain the operational realities of policing in plain language, bridge between institutional knowledge and resident experience, and translate community concerns into policy-relevant terms. His history as a D.A.R.E. instructor and RCMP School Community Liaison reflects a long pattern of community-police bridge-building that preceded and informs his councillor role.

He maintains an active Facebook page, focuses consistently on Ward 3 priorities, and has been a sustained advocate on flooding and the North End Community Centre over multiple terms.

A planning committee appointment episode is a significant failure in this category. His Ward 3 town halls, constituent responsiveness, and safety-focused outreach are genuine contributions. But voting to block a vetted community activist from the Municipal Plan Review Committee — specifically because she had criticized council publicly — is a direct failure of community representation. The 'same wavelength' comment is particularly revealing: it frames community engagement as acceptable only when it affirms council's direction.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
Butler's most substantive oversight contribution was his pre-vote advocacy on the RCMP decision: he called for a workload analysis of existing officers before adding new ones, questioned the evidentiary basis for expanding a service the city was simultaneously reviewing, and argued for extending the decision timeline to gather more complete data. That is rigorous oversight on a $57M question.

His concern about intergovernmental accountability on housing funding — asking who was responsible for delivering on federal commitments — reflects a legitimate fiscal scrutiny instinct that extended beyond the policing file.

However, his vote against the integrity commissioner limits the city's systemic oversight capacity, and his Social Inclusion Committee resignation removed him from an oversight role during a critical period. There is no documented evidence of comprehensive budget scrutiny, forensic spending reviews, or systematic challenge of staff reports beyond the policing file. His oversight is strong and credible in his areas of expertise, and noticeably thinner elsewhere.

councillors.term_info: 2021–2025 · Elected 2016, 2021 · Deputy Mayor May 2023 – May 2024 · Announced mayoral candidacy for 2026

councillors.overall_assessment:
Shawn Crossman is a dedicated, community-first councillor whose personal story lends particular weight to his public service. Diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2018, he continued active council duties through treatment, founded the Moncton Myeloma Support Group and the annual Moncton Myeloma March, and emerged as an even more engaged public servant. That kind of perseverance in the face of serious illness, in service of a community, is remarkable on its own terms.

His strongest policy contribution is the seniors centre project — personally meeting with over 80 seniors, co-drafting a motion, and securing $1.7 million in city funding for a new Limerick Street facility. That represents the complete arc of good constituent work: deep listening, policy translation, coalition-building, and a concrete result that serves a specific, underserved population.

The limitations are in institutional consistency. His advocacy for accountability on specific issues — the Moncton High School heritage development, the Deputy Mayor conflict-of-interest question — sits uncomfortably alongside his vote against the integrity commissioner that would deliver accountability systematically. He connects well with people but struggles to translate that connection into consistent influence at the council table on major city-wide decisions. His mayoral candidacy for 2026 is a bet that his community-first approach can scale.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No code of conduct violations were filed against Crossman during this term. His service as Deputy Mayor from May 2023 to May 2024, and his designation as Deputy Mayor designate in March 2025, reflect peer confidence in his professional conduct in a formal leadership role.

His conduct through his cancer diagnosis and treatment — continuing public service without complaint and founding support organizations during recovery — speaks to personal character that extends well beyond the council chamber. The Moncton Myeloma Support Group and Moncton Myeloma March are lasting community contributions that emerged from the most difficult period of his life.

The limiting concern is the 2019 integrity commissioner vote. Crossman has positioned himself as an accountability advocate — demanding transparency on the High School development, raising conflict-of-interest concerns about colleagues — while voting against the independent, institutional mechanism that would deliver accountability without requiring a councillor to personally champion each case. That inconsistency is not a conduct violation, but it reveals a tension in his approach to governance.

Crossman voted to reject the entire slate of Municipal Plan Review Committee candidates at the August 19, 2024 meeting, contributing to the exclusion of a vetted community activist who had been recommended by city staff. Unlike colleagues Bourgeois, Butler, Thériault, Richard, and Kingston, Crossman did not document his opposition via email — but his vote aligned with theirs. His post-vote framing was deflective: 'the process is broken,' he said, pointing to the short notice councillors received before the vote. That complaint may have merit as a process concern, but it does not account for why the same names were rejected again in September. Combined with the existing conduct record, this vote moves the grade down from B-.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
Crossman has been a vocal and sometimes effective transparency advocate on specific issues. His challenge to the Moncton High School heritage building development — pushing back on what he characterized as a secretive proposal by Terra Trust and Bird Construction — showed willingness to name problematic processes in public. His raising of conflict-of-interest concerns about Deputy Mayor Blair Lawrence's wife's role with the Moncton Library demonstrated attention to governance boundaries.

He is generally transparent about his own policy positions and voting rationale — willing to explain his minority votes and defend his positions in public forums. His bilingual social media presence gives Francophone Ward 1 constituents direct access to his reasoning on issues.

The fundamental limitation is the integrity commissioner vote. Council's 2019 rejection of an independent oversight mechanism — which Crossman supported — means that transparency advocacy remains ad hoc and personality-dependent rather than institutionally guaranteed. You cannot credibly position yourself as a transparency champion while voting against the infrastructure that makes transparency structural rather than optional.

On the religious symbols file, Crossman publicly stated he voted against the motion to remove the menorah and nativity scene in the private session — a meaningful disclosure that placed him on the right side of that episode before the public reaction made the correct position obvious.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
The seniors centre project is Crossman's signature achievement: a full-cycle initiative from grassroots consultation (personally meeting with 80+ seniors across the community) through co-drafted motion, council approval, land acquisition, and $1.7 million in city funding for a new facility on Limerick Street. This is what effective ward advocacy looks like — starting with community listening and finishing with a concrete institution that serves residents for years to come.

His championing of rapid housing initiative projects resulted in 46 new affordable homes and over $6.7 million in federal funding reaching Moncton — a tangible housing outcome on a file where many municipalities have struggled to move beyond advocacy.

As a DMCI board member, he introduced a $180,000 contribution to a downtown cleanup project that collected 62,000 pounds of garbage in 60 days — a visible, measurable result. He supported the unanimous vote for 33 surveillance cameras on St. George Street.

The Bridge to Home Centre lease termination motion in September 2024 is more complicated. His underlying concerns about crime and drug use in the area were legitimate and reflected real constituent frustration. But the motion — ultimately modified rather than passed — raised questions about whether his approach to homelessness policy balances service provision with enforcement, and whether a motion to terminate was the right tool for a complex social problem.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
Crossman demonstrates genuine collaborative ability when he chooses to engage it. The seniors centre project involved productive co-development with Councillor Bourgeois — a working relationship that transcended the significant interpersonal difficulties that surrounded Bourgeois on this council. The St. George Street cameras passed unanimously, indicating effective coalition-building on a public safety initiative. His selection as Deputy Mayor by council peers, with unanimous support for his designation in 2025, reflects sustained institutional trust.

He serves on multiple committees including Poverty and Social Inclusion, Internal Audit, and the DMCI board, suggesting genuine investment in collaborative governance processes rather than selective participation.

The persistent limitation is his position on major divisive votes. He consistently ended up in the minority on the RCMP decision, the Bridge to Home controversy, and several other significant votes — not because of principled isolation, but because he was unable to build the winning coalition despite his community connections. Being persuasive in one-on-one conversations and at town halls does not automatically translate into persuasiveness at the council table, and that gap appears in his record.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
The seniors centre consultation stands as a model of meaningful constituent engagement. Personally meeting with over 80 seniors across the community — not a survey, not a feedback form, but face-to-face conversations — to understand what a new facility should be and where it should go is the kind of work that most councillors describe but few do at that depth. It produced not just a policy motion but a genuinely community-designed outcome.

His volunteer record is substantial: Lewisville Minor Hockey, Big Brothers Big Sisters, St. Bernard's Church, and the myeloma support organizations he founded post-diagnosis. This is a councillor with deep roots in the community he serves, roots that predate his election and will outlast his council tenure.

He maintains an active bilingual social media presence and a personal website with policy information, serving the Francophone population of Ward 1 in their preferred language. The bilingual dimension of his engagement is not cosmetic — it reflects genuine accessibility for a community that sometimes finds municipal government operates primarily in English.

The Bridge to Home Centre controversy represents a community engagement challenge: residents near the centre raised legitimate safety concerns, but the homeless population served by the centre is also part of the community Crossman represents. Navigating those competing constituent interests with compassion is harder than responding to a single constituency.

A planning committee appointment vote creates a sharp internal contradiction in Crossman's engagement record. A councillor who held 80+ individual meetings with seniors to inform the community centre project — an exemplary act of grassroots consultation — voted to block a vetted community activist from the Municipal Plan Review Committee because her public commentary on council decisions was unwelcome. Those two acts represent opposite approaches to community engagement, and they sit in the same term.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
Crossman sits on the Internal Audit Committee — an oversight role that, if engaged seriously, represents a meaningful accountability function. He has questioned public safety spending recommendations, arguing publicly that mental health and addiction services should take priority over additional bylaw enforcement officers — a substantive fiscal and policy argument. He advocated for public consultations on the RCMP decision.

However, the record does not show the kind of detailed, forensic scrutiny that characterizes the strongest council watchdogs. He does not appear to regularly challenge staff reports or demand evidentiary support before approving expenditures. His vote against the integrity commissioner limits the city's systemic accountability infrastructure.

The Bridge to Home Centre motion also illustrates an oversight gap: effective oversight requires due diligence before action, and there is limited evidence that Crossman independently verified the service delivery claims about the centre before filing a motion to terminate the lease. Reacting to community complaints is legitimate; but transforming them into policy proposals without independent verification is a different matter.

councillors.overall_assessment:
Paul Richard is a principled, equity-minded first-term councillor whose most significant contribution — moving the original motion to review Moncton's policing services in 2021 — set in motion a multi-year accountability exercise that this council needed to undertake regardless of the outcome. The fact that the resulting review concluded the opposite of what Richard advocated for does not diminish the democratic value of insisting the question be asked and answered properly.

His Ward 4 advocacy reflects a genuine equity orientation. His argument for locating the new aquatics centre in the Parkton area — "there are kids there that don't have, won't have, the opportunity to go places like Centennial Park" — reflects a vision of public infrastructure as a redistributive tool that is more explicit and more principled than most councillors offer on facility location debates.

The limitation is coalition-building. A 10-1 dissenting vote on McLaughlin Road rezoning, a consistent minority position across multiple major decisions, and an inability to build the cross-ward relationships needed to move outcomes in his direction all suggest a councillor who is frequently right on the merits but unable to translate good reasoning into winning votes. That gap between judgment and influence is the defining challenge for any potential second term.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No code of conduct violations were found against Richard during this term. His long career at NB Power — 32+ years — provides a professional grounding, and his council conduct is measured and substantive. He engages in debates with reasoned, specific arguments rather than rhetorical posturing.

In 2021, he publicly shared his personal COVID-19 experience and encouraged community testing — using his public platform for a community health purpose during a period of genuine public anxiety. It is a small act but it reflects an instinct to use elected office for community benefit beyond the strictly legislative.

His explanation of his 10-1 dissent on the McLaughlin Road rezoning — objecting to development notices sent over the holiday period when residents had limited ability to respond — reflects attention to procedural fairness rather than reflexive opposition.

A planning committee appointment episode introduces a meaningful deduction to Richard's otherwise steady conduct record. He was among the first councillors to respond to Bourgeois's opposition email, writing simply: 'I agree with both of you. I was surprised to see her name on the list.' — referring to a local community activist whose application had been recommended by city staff. He then voted to reject the entire slate at the August 19 meeting. The email is telling in its brevity — Richard apparently found it self-evident that a vocal council critic should be disqualified from a volunteer advisory role. That position conflicts with basic democratic norms around citizen participation, and the grade reflects it.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
Richard provides clear, articulate rationales for his voting positions in public debates, including dissenting votes where the political cost of explanation is highest. His McLaughlin Road objection — that holiday-period notices deprived residents of meaningful opportunity to engage with a major development decision — names a specific procedural failure rather than offering vague opposition.

On the RCMP vote, he was part of the minority arguing for more time and more data: "I'd rather wait and hear back from the committee to make a well-informed decision." That posture — demanding evidence before committing to a major spending decision — is a model of evidence-based transparency.

His media footprint is relatively modest compared to some colleagues, which limits the public visibility of his reasoning on issues beyond the major votes that attract journalist attention. He maintains a website and Instagram presence, but the depth of constituent communication falls short of the proactive, detailed reporting that the strongest performers provide.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
Richard's most significant initiative is the policing services review motion in 2021, which he co-moved with Bourgeois. A unanimous council vote to conduct a formal, multi-year review of whether Moncton should continue with RCMP or establish its own municipal force is a consequential institutional accountability exercise — regardless of the outcome. The review itself was a necessary and overdue examination, and Richard was the primary mover.

His Ward 4 advocacy shows a consistent equity orientation. He pushed for the aquatics centre to serve the Parkton area specifically, making an explicit argument about geographic equity and accessibility for lower-income residents. He sought traffic-calming measures in Ward 4 during the 2025 budget process.

The limitation is scale and outcome. His policing review produced a result he opposed. His pool location argument did not prevail. His McLaughlin Road dissent was a 10-1 minority. Being the initiator of important questions does not guarantee influence over the answers, and Richard's first term reflects a pattern of strong instincts that consistently struggle to find majority support.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
Richard collaborated productively with the policing-minority bloc — Crossman, Bourgeois, Léger, and Butler — forming a coherent coalition on the RCMP review process question even if it ultimately fell one vote short. His community volunteer work with Lewisville Minor Hockey Association and the Boys and Girls Club suggests relationship-building skills that extend beyond the institutional.

The pattern of minority votes is the defining concern in this category. The McLaughlin Road 10-1 dissent is the most striking data point: a 10-1 vote means that Richard could not persuade even one other colleague, on a planning decision with reasonable grounds for concern. That is not simply being in the minority on a contentious issue — it suggests a fundamental difficulty in the persuasion and coalition-building that legislative effectiveness requires.

For a first-term councillor still learning the dynamics of a divided council, some of this is understandable. But the pattern is consistent enough to be a genuine limitation rather than an outlier.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
Richard's Ward 4 engagement is focused and equity-oriented. His aquatics centre argument was explicitly about the Parkton area — a specific, named neighbourhood between Mountain Road and Wheeler Boulevard — and the kids who live there. That kind of geographic specificity in constituent advocacy is more meaningful than general support for recreational infrastructure.

His long NB Power career roots him in the working community of Moncton in ways that professional politicians often lack. He understands the lives of working families in Ward 4 from lived experience rather than political positioning.

He maintains a website and Instagram presence, volunteering with Lewisville Minor Hockey and the Boys and Girls Club — organizations that connect him to the youth and families of his ward in direct, non-political ways.

The limitation is breadth. His documented constituent engagement is concentrated on specific ward issues — the pool, traffic, specific developments — without evidence of proactive ward-wide consultation on the broader direction of Ward 4's development. A town hall or structured ward consultation mechanism would strengthen the engagement record considerably.

A planning committee appointment vote is the clearest failure in Richard's community engagement record. His Ward 4 work — particularly the equity argument around the aquatics centre serving the Parkton area — reflects a councillor who can think broadly about who the city serves. Voting to exclude a vetted community activist from the Municipal Plan Review Committee because of her public criticism of council sits in direct tension with that instinct.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
Initiating the policing services review is Richard's most significant oversight contribution. Forcing a formal, multi-year institutional examination of a $50M+ annual public safety expenditure is exactly what council oversight is for, regardless of what the review concluded. The process itself — evidence gathering, external review, public reporting — was an accountability exercise the city needed.

His demand for more analysis and public consultation before the final RCMP vote, and his procedural objection to the McLaughlin Road holiday notices, both reflect attention to process integrity that is a form of governance oversight.

The limitation is that his scrutiny is concentrated in a few areas. There is no evidence of comprehensive budget scrutiny, challenge of staff reports on issues outside his focus areas, or requests for independent review of department performance. For a first-term councillor, depth in one or two areas is understandable, but the overall oversight function falls short of what the strongest performers deliver.

councillors.overall_assessment:
Paulette Thériault's legacy in Moncton is most visible in the cultural institutions she helped build. Founding the Northrop Frye International Literary Festival in 1999 — which earned the Lieutenant Governor's Dialogue Award in 2005 and has grown into a nationally recognized event — and directing the restoration of the Aberdeen Cultural Centre are contributions that will outlast her council tenure by decades. These are not small achievements in the life of a mid-sized Canadian city.

Her election as Deputy Mayor in 2024 and her elevation to Acting Mayor following Arnold's Senate appointment reflect the institutional trust that four terms of steady, professional service have earned. She committed publicly to "staying the course" — a governing posture that values continuity and stability over disruption, appropriate for a caretaker role.

The honest assessment, however, is that Thériault's policy footprint beyond the cultural sphere is narrower than her seniority and experience would suggest. Her fourth term did not produce a signature policy achievement outside of arts and culture, her oversight record reflects participation more than initiative, and her decision not to seek re-election in 2026 closes a chapter whose most memorable chapters were written long before this term began.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
Four consecutive terms on council, election as Deputy Mayor in 2024, and elevation to Acting Mayor in 2025 represent sustained peer and voter confidence in Thériault's professional conduct. No code of conduct investigations were found in the public record during this term.

The one documented concern is a 2017 incident in which she left a council meeting visibly frustrated during a contentious debate about renaming Parc René-Arthur Fréchet and the Moncton High School development proposal. Walking out of a meeting is not a code violation, but it is an unusual public display of frustration from a long-serving councillor, and it raises a question about stress management in adversarial moments. The Acting Mayor role she later assumed requires navigating difficult council dynamics as a facilitator rather than a participant — a harder task that demands exactly the steady composure under pressure that the 2017 episode questioned.

On balance, the overwhelming weight of four terms of professional service outweighs a single documented moment of frustration, and the grade reflects that balance.

A planning committee appointment episode is the most significant conduct failure in Thériault's record this term. She was the second councillor to respond to Bourgeois's opposition email, writing: 'Merci Daniel. Totally in agreement. She treats us like the lowest. I find it painful listening to her and her lack of respect for us as elected officials.' She then voted to reject the full slate of candidates. The email reveals a framing that treats citizens' criticism of council decisions as personal disrespect — and treats a volunteer advisory committee as a space reserved for friendly voices. Four terms of generally steady conduct absorb this, but it cannot go unaccounted for.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
Thériault voted with the majority to keep the RCMP without public consultation in March 2024 — a significant transparency concern for a councillor who would soon take on the Acting Mayor role. The 6-5 vote rejected a proposal for community input before finalizing a major policing decision, and Thériault's position placed her on the side that limited public scrutiny on a consequential question.

Her voting record is publicly available and she participated in open budget deliberations. But the standard for transparency extends beyond having votes on record — it includes actively ensuring that major decisions receive appropriate public input before they are made, and Thériault's record here is passive rather than proactive.

The December 2025 review that found Moncton's private meetings bylaw did not meet provincial requirements occurred during the period when Thériault was serving as Acting Mayor. While the legal gap predated her caretaker tenure, it is a governance failure that falls within the mayor's office responsibility to identify and address.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
Thériault's signature contributions to Moncton were established in prior terms: founding the Northrop Frye International Literary Festival in 1999 and directing the restoration of the Aberdeen Cultural Centre are achievements that have shaped Moncton's cultural identity for a generation. These are not small accomplishments — the Frye Festival earned provincial recognition through the Lieutenant Governor's Dialogue Award and has become a fixture of the city's cultural calendar.

During this term, she co-introduced the guaranteed livable basic income motion with Léger, which passed unanimously — a genuine policy achievement that demonstrates the ability to work on a broad coalition for a progressive proposal. She voted in favour of the 4-unit housing zoning change that unlocked $15.5M in federal Housing Accelerator funding, supported the 2025 budget with its tax rate reduction, and participated in the multi-year policing review process.

The limitation is scope. Outside of arts and culture, her fourth-term policy footprint is narrower than the seniority and platform of a four-term councillor would suggest. Her Acting Mayor role is primarily administrative — maintaining continuity rather than setting new direction — which is appropriate for a caretaker but limits what can be attributed to her as an initiator.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
The trust that council placed in Thériault — first as Deputy Mayor in 2024, then as Acting Mayor from March 2025 — is the most meaningful evidence of her collaborative relationships. In a council that was divided on multiple major issues, being chosen to lead is a form of endorsement that requires support from colleagues across different factions.

Her collaborative approach is characterized by institutional steadiness rather than dynamic coalition-building. She does not appear to broker contentious deals or bridge divides in visible ways, but she maintains professional relationships across the council table that allowed her to assume leadership roles when they were needed.

The co-introduction of the basic income motion with Léger demonstrates cross-council partnership on a substantive policy question. Her overall posture — steady, professional, non-confrontational — is itself a collaborative style, even if it does not produce the visible consensus-building moments that some colleagues demonstrate.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
Thériault's community engagement is strongest through the cultural institutions she has built over her career. The Frye Festival and the Aberdeen Cultural Centre represent sustained investment in Moncton's community life that extends far beyond Ward 1. As Acting Mayor, she identified poverty and homelessness as personal priorities and Radio-Canada described her as having "good credibility thanks to many years on municipal council" — a meaningful characterization in the Francophone media context.

However, there is limited documented evidence of Ward 1-specific constituent engagement beyond her cultural work during this term. The Lewisville industrial park — an environmental concern dating to 2008 that forced a francophone elementary school to relocate in 2016 — remains unresolved. While this is a complex, multi-jurisdictional issue that no single councillor can fix unilaterally, a fourth-term councillor representing the affected ward might be expected to have maintained more visible sustained advocacy.

Her decision not to seek re-election in 2026 likely reduced her engagement energy in the final months of the term, a common dynamic for outgoing incumbents.

A planning committee appointment episode is the most significant failure in this category. Thériault's cultural legacy — the Frye Festival, the Farmers Market, arts advocacy over four terms — represents real community building. But participating in the exclusion of a vetted community activist from the Municipal Plan Review Committee, on the basis that her public criticism of council was 'painful' to hear, is a failure of community representation. Engagement that only extends to citizens who agree with council's decisions is not genuine engagement.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
This is Thériault's weakest category by evidence. She participated in budget debates and the multi-year policing review, but the public record shows limited evidence of her proactively challenging budget proposals, requesting additional staff reports, demanding data before major decisions, or asking the pointed questions that characterize strong oversight.

She voted against public consultation before the final RCMP decision — limiting community scrutiny of a major policing commitment. The 2025 review finding that the city's private meetings bylaw failed to meet provincial requirements occurred during her tenure as Acting Mayor and represents a governance oversight failure on her watch, however briefly.

The absence of a documented scrutiny pattern does not necessarily mean Thériault is not engaged behind the scenes — committee work and budget review happen in ways that are not always publicly visible. But the evaluable public record does not support a grade higher than C for a councillor who has had four terms to establish a visible oversight presence.

councillors.overall_assessment:
Susan Edgett is a professionally competent second-term councillor with a genuinely impressive pre-council record of community leadership: first female president of the Moncton Rotary Club, chair of the Codiac Regional Police Authority, race director for Legs for Literacy. These are substantive, credentialed roles that reflect sustained community investment over many years.

The honest challenge in assessing Edgett is that her council tenure has not been characterized by the kind of visible initiative, policy leadership, or proactive scrutiny that her community credentials and second-term seniority would suggest. The public record shows a councillor who participates consistently and professionally in governance processes without pushing beyond baseline requirements. There is no signature initiative, no defining policy achievement, and limited evidence of the kind of probing oversight that the strongest council performers demonstrate.

This assessment may understate contributions that happen outside the public record — a genuine limitation of any external evaluation. But the evaluable evidence supports a conclusion of solid participation without visible leadership.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No code of conduct complaints or allegations were found against Edgett during this term. Her consistent participation in council meetings and debates reflects a professional approach to the role.

Her community background is substantial and well-documented: she was the first female president of the Moncton Rotary Club, chaired the Codiac Regional Police Authority, and served as race director for Legs for Literacy. These are positions that require and demonstrate professional credibility, organizational leadership, and community standing that predates and extends beyond her council role.

Edgett carries herself with a quiet professionalism throughout council proceedings. In a term marked by two formal code of conduct violations involving a colleague, and considerable interpersonal friction on divisive votes, a clean record paired with sustained professional engagement is worth noting explicitly.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
Edgett's voting record is publicly documented through council minutes and the city's Open Data portal. She participates consistently in open council proceedings and cast votes on all major issues including the RCMP decision, the religious symbols controversy, and major development approvals.

However, she voted with the majority to keep the RCMP without public consultation — part of the 6-5 decision that rejected community input on a significant policing question. She was part of the council that made the initial closed-door religious symbols decision before the public reversal.

The transparency record is adequate in a procedural sense — her votes are on record, her participation is documented — but it is passive rather than proactive. There is limited evidence of Edgett publicly advocating for greater transparency on specific decisions, pushing for additional public engagement processes, or proactively communicating her reasoning beyond what council proceedings formally require.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
This is where Edgett's public record is thinnest relative to her experience and potential. Her stated priorities — "healthy and active living" and "welcoming newcomers" — are consistent with her background but there is limited documented evidence of major initiatives she personally championed during this term that advanced those priorities in concrete policy terms.

She supported the RCMP continuation motion, voted in favour of the youth group home rezoning (7-3 vote) — showing willingness to support socially beneficial projects despite neighbourhood opposition — and participated in the policing review process. These are legitimate council contributions, but they are votes rather than initiatives.

For a second-term councillor with Edgett's pre-council credentials, the expectation of a visible policy footprint is reasonable. Her background chairing the Codiac Regional Police Authority, for example, positioned her to be a uniquely informed voice on the policing review — but that expertise does not appear to have translated into a distinctive public contribution on the file's most contested questions.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
Edgett works constructively within council's institutional structures. She was nominated for Deputy Mayor in 2022 — losing to Butler 4-7 — which indicates a meaningful level of peer support even without winning. She tends to vote with the majority on major decisions, which reflects either collaborative alignment or, less charitably, limited willingness to take unpopular positions.

Her support for the youth group home rezoning against neighbourhood opposition shows willingness to take a principled position on a socially important issue even when it is politically inconvenient. That is a meaningful data point in an otherwise quiet collaboration record.

There are no documented interpersonal conflicts with colleagues, no pattern of isolation in minority positions, and no evidence of coalition-building failures. The collaboration profile is steady and unremarkable — present and constructive, without the visible moments of alliance-building or consensus-making that distinguish the strongest performers.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
Edgett's community credentials are well-established and genuine: Rotary Club presidency, police authority chair, literacy advocacy. These represent real community investment over many years.

As a Ward 4 councillor, she has participated in city-wide initiatives including the policing review, public safety planning, and development decisions. Her stated priority of welcoming newcomers is contextually relevant during a period of record immigration to Moncton.

The gap is between her pre-council community engagement (which is substantial) and her documented constituent engagement as a sitting councillor (which is thin in the public record). A councillor's community standing before election is different from their engagement while serving — the role requires ongoing, active outreach in the ward, and there is limited evidence of structured Ward 4 engagement activities, community consultations, or proactive constituent communication during this term.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
Edgett's background as former chair of the Codiac Regional Police Authority gives her relevant institutional experience in policing oversight. She was part of the multi-year policing review process from 2021 to 2024, participating in a scrutiny process that the council needed to complete.

However, there is limited public evidence of Edgett proactively challenging budget proposals, requesting additional information before votes, demanding data from staff, or asking the kind of pointed questions that characterize the strongest council watchdogs. She voted against public consultation on the RCMP decision — limiting one avenue of community scrutiny on a major question.

The strongest oversight performers on this council read deeply, question assumptions, and are willing to make staff uncomfortable with their scrutiny. That pattern is not visible in Edgett's public record. Her oversight contribution appears to be participation in existing processes rather than active interrogation of them.
