councillors.overall_assessment:
Monique LeBlanc brings extraordinary life experience to the council chamber: physiotherapist, educator, business owner, former provincial MLA with experience as Government Caucus Chair, Deputy Speaker, and Opposition Critic. Her personal character was demonstrated with unusual clarity in December 2023, when she rushed to help a man experiencing a drug overdose on St. George Street — administering Naloxone while waiting for paramedics, and returning the next day to check on his recovery. That act reveals someone whose public service instinct extends well beyond electoral politics.

The frustrating reality is that her council tenure has not translated this considerable personal and professional capacity into a visible policy footprint. There is no signature initiative, no defining policy campaign, and limited evidence of the proactive community engagement or scrutiny function that a councillor-at-large — representing the entire city rather than a specific ward — should demonstrate.

The precedent from her MLA career is instructive and somewhat concerning: as MLA for Moncton East from 2014 to 2020, she spent none of her allocated $50,000 community investment funding, citing difficulty finding projects that met program criteria. Whether that reflects program design failures or a broader pattern of difficulty translating institutional resources into community action is a legitimate question her council record does not decisively answer.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No code of conduct violations were found against LeBlanc during this term. Her professional background is extensive: a practicing physiotherapist, educator, business owner (Sport Med Acadie), and former provincial MLA with senior legislative roles including Government Caucus Chair, Deputy Speaker, and Opposition Critic. This breadth of professional experience provides a strong foundation for council work.

The Naloxone incident in December 2023 deserves specific recognition. When LeBlanc encountered a man experiencing an overdose on St. George Street, she did not call for help and wait — she administered Naloxone herself, stayed until paramedics arrived, and returned the following day to check on his recovery. For an elected official, this act demonstrates that public service is not a role she sets aside when it becomes inconvenient. It is a meaningful statement of character.

One absence from a boundary expansion bylaw vote in October 2022 is documented in the public record, a minor concern.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
LeBlanc's voting record is publicly documented and she participates in open council proceedings. But there is limited evidence of detailed public explanation of her reasoning on controversial votes or proactive transparency initiatives beyond standard council participation.

On the 2021 amalgamation discussion, she characterized the issue as a "hot potato" without offering a clear public position — a missed opportunity to inform constituents on a significant governance question. Her positions on municipal reform remained vague throughout the term.

She voted with the majority (6-5) to keep the RCMP without public consultation in March 2024. For a councillor-at-large who nominally represents all Moncton residents, voting against a public consultation process on a major policing decision is a specific transparency concern — it prioritizes institutional expediency over community voice on a question that affects everyone she was elected to serve.

There is no evidence of LeBlanc hosting public consultations, publishing regular constituent newsletters, or proactively communicating her council activity in ways that would allow city-wide constituents to evaluate her work.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
LeBlanc served on the Crime Reduction Committee, the Youth Advisory Committee, and as a council appointee to the Codiac Regional Policing Authority. These are legitimate committee roles that involve real governance work. She voted on significant matters including the RCMP decision, major zoning approvals, and the religious symbols reversal.

However, the public record contains limited evidence of LeBlanc initiating major policy motions, championing legislative proposals, or driving substantive policy campaigns. Her council contribution appears primarily reactive — evaluating and voting on proposals from administration, staff, or other councillors rather than advancing her own agenda.

The MLA precedent is relevant context. During her six years as MLA for Moncton East, she spent none of her $50,000 annual community investment funding allocation, which CBC News reported in 2020. Her explanation — difficulty finding projects that met program criteria — describes a real administrative challenge, but it also describes a pattern of difficulty translating available institutional resources into community action. The council term does not clearly contradict that pattern.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
LeBlanc participates in committee structures and aligns consistently with Mayor Arnold on major votes. She supported the youth group home rezoning alongside only two other councillors — a decision that required willingness to stand with a socially important but unpopular project against significant neighbourhood opposition.

Her provincial legislative experience — including work as Government Caucus Chair, a fundamentally collaborative role — suggests developed skills in institutional consensus-building.

However, she is occasionally in minority positions on development issues and her collaboration appears to operate primarily within established committee structures rather than through independent coalition-building. There is no evidence of LeBlanc brokering contentious agreements, bridging council factions, or championing compromise positions on the major divisive votes of the term.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
LeBlanc brings more than 30 years of community involvement in health, sports, culture, women's rights, social housing, poverty, and environmental advocacy. The Naloxone incident demonstrates direct personal engagement with the hardest community challenges — not watching from a safe distance, but acting in the street. Her Youth Advisory Committee participation shows engagement with younger residents.

As a councillor-at-large, she is responsible for representing the entire city rather than a specific ward — a mandate that requires proactive, city-wide engagement rather than ward-level constituency service. The documented record of structured community engagement during the 2021-2025 term is thin: no evidence of regular newsletters, sustained social media engagement strategies, community forums, or public reporting on her council activity. For someone representing all of Moncton, the absence of a systematic constituent communication program is a meaningful gap.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
LeBlanc served on the Codiac Regional Policing Authority, providing formal oversight of policing services, and participated in the multi-year policing review. She served on the Crime Reduction Committee, which was tasked with filing a report on public safety improvements. She voted against some questionable development approvals, opposing the Elmwood Drive subdivisions that overrode staff anti-sprawl recommendations.

However, she voted with the majority to keep the RCMP without public consultation — limiting community oversight of a major policing decision despite serving on the policing authority. The Crime Reduction Committee's report, due by mid-to-late March 2024, has no documented public outcome or follow-up in available media coverage.

There is no evidence of LeBlanc requesting independent audits, conducting forensic reviews, or systematically challenging administration on budget or program questions. Despite her policing authority experience, she did not use that institutional knowledge to push for the more rigorous pre-vote analysis that some colleagues demanded. Her oversight profile is characterized by participation rather than active scrutiny.

councillors.overall_assessment:
Daniel Bourgeois is the most contradictory figure on this council, and evaluating him honestly requires holding two things simultaneously: he is a genuine intellectual asset whose rigorous scrutiny and policy initiative have produced real outcomes, and he is a councillor whose conduct and collaboration failures have systematically undermined those same contributions.

On the positive ledger: the Vision Lands park is a significant, patient initiative that moved from an ambitious $25M motion in 2022 through a pragmatic federal urban parks application, and by late 2025 was moving forward with $500,000 in the 2026 budget for land acquisition. The tax rate cap he championed has contributed to multiple consecutive years of residential tax cuts. He moved the policing services review motion that launched a necessary multi-year accountability exercise. He brings a PhD in Public Policy Analysis and 27 peer-reviewed publications to a council role that benefits from exactly that kind of evidence-based scrutiny.

On the negative ledger: two code of conduct violations in a single term — one involving disparaging remarks about a volunteer committee member, one involving disrespectful behaviour toward senior staff — are not isolated incidents. They are a pattern. His decade-long refusal to engage with major media outlets creates a transparency gap that is particularly ironic given his institutional advocacy for openness. His housing grant motion failed for lack of a seconder; a motion on the Urban Growth Strategy went unsupported entirely; he was the sole vote against the Vision Lands agreement that was implementing his own park proposal. The qualities that make him an effective watchdog appear to be the same qualities that, unchecked, prevent him from being an effective colleague.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
The conduct record for Bourgeois during this term is documented and clear, and it is serious. Two formal code of conduct violations in a single four-year term represent a pattern that cannot be characterized as isolated incidents.

The first violation, in October 2021, arose from remarks Bourgeois made about Carole Chan — a volunteer member of the Enhancing Democracy Committee — during a public meeting. A follow-up email to council attributed statements to Chan that meeting recordings indicate she did not make. The investigation found the code had been violated; Bourgeois was directed to issue a written apology and complete an interpersonal relationships training course. Committee members reported they considered resigning because of the incident — a significant measure of the harm done to a volunteer body.

The second violation, in May 2025, involved his behaviour toward senior city staff during a debate about downtown parking. The investigation found his tone and conduct crossed from legitimate political challenge into disrespectful treatment of staff. He was issued a formal reprimand with an explicit warning that future violations would be treated cumulatively, with heavier sanctions. The original complaint also alleged a broader pattern of intimidation toward staff and elected officials, particularly women; that broader allegation was found to be unsubstantiated.

Beyond the violations, Bourgeois has refused to speak to CBC News and several other major media outlets since 2014 — over a decade of media disengagement from the primary journalism organizations covering Moncton city government. For a public official who campaigns on institutional transparency, the personal irony of this position is significant. When asked to comment on his most recent conduct sanction, he declined, citing the boycott.

A planning committee appointment episode adds further evidence to a pattern already well-documented in this category. Bourgeois was the architect of the opposition: he sent the first and most emphatic email (publicly documented as 'I emphatically oppose Kate Doyle's appointment'), framed the applicant's criticism of his own Eastgate vote as evidence of 'rigid bias,' and later argued that leaving her name on the list would force council to vote against all candidates — effectively making her the reason the entire process had to restart. His grade here was already at the floor; this incident reinforces the pattern it reflects.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
Bourgeois's institutional transparency advocacy is genuine and substantive. He has pressed for clearer reporting on city over-expenditures, challenged the format in which financial data is presented to council, and explicitly campaigned on the premise that council is not sufficiently open with residents about how decisions are made and taxes are spent. He has been willing to explain dissenting votes clearly and in detail — his rationale for opposing the $57M RCMP station (complete the policing review before committing to a building for a force you might not keep) was articulate and well-reasoned.

He delivered his 2021 apology publicly at a council meeting, which shows some capacity for public accountability, even if the apology came nearly a month after the incident and only after media reporting had brought it to widespread attention.

The fundamental tension in this category is between his institutional positions and his personal conduct as a public figure. A councillor who advocates for openness while refusing to speak to major media outlets for over a decade is not fully inhabiting the transparency values he professes. Residents who rely on local journalism to understand what their councillor thinks cannot access Bourgeois's views through the primary channels through which public officials communicate. The grade reflects genuine institutional transparency advocacy offset by significant personal transparency limitations.

Late in the term — and during the 2025 municipal election campaign — Bourgeois appeared on CBC Information Morning Moncton to discuss the crime reduction and prevention committee's report. This is worth noting because Bourgeois had been on record since at least 2021 as someone who does not speak to CBC or several other media outlets, a position he maintained consistently through much of this term. The appearance is a positive data point: he engaged publicly with a substantive policy file on a platform he had previously refused. However, the timing is difficult to ignore. Breaking a years-long media silence during campaign season raises a reasonable question about whether this reflects a genuine shift toward transparency or a calculated decision to reach voters ahead of an election. Credit is warranted; so is the caveat.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
This is where Bourgeois's contributions are most clearly documented and most clearly meaningful. He is not a passive vote-caster — he has initiated policy across his council career, and this term produced at least one significant, patient, multi-year achievement.

The Vision Lands park is the defining initiative. In 2022, he proposed setting aside land along the North Branch of Halls Creek for a major park — initially a $25M, five-year capital budget motion that was too ambitious in that form. Rather than abandoning the idea when the original motion was too large, he adapted it: he amended his approach to explore the federal National Urban Parks Program, a motion that passed unanimously. By late 2025, the development was moving forward with parkland protected, and the 2026 budget allocated $500,000 toward land purchases. That is a multi-year initiative that went from ambitious motion to adaptation to funded outcome — the full arc of effective policy work.

More broadly, the tax rate cap he championed over his council career has contributed to multiple consecutive years of residential tax reductions — a structural fiscal achievement. He co-moved the policing services review motion with Richard in 2021, launching a multi-year accountability exercise that the city needed to undertake. During 2025 budget deliberations, he challenged the hiring of 17 additional RCMP officers on fiscal and public safety grounds, prompting council to commit to a future meeting on the role of municipalities in addressing social issues.

The self-limiting dynamic is real: a motion that receives no seconder, being the sole vote against a Vision Lands agreement that was implementing his own proposal, and a housing grant motion that died for lack of support all demonstrate that his effectiveness is periodically undercut by his isolation from colleagues.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
The collaboration and relationship record is where Bourgeois's pattern of difficulties is most consistently documented. The data points accumulate across the term in a way that is difficult to attribute to principled independence rather than genuine relational failure.

His housing grant motion failed because nobody would second it — not a close vote, but a complete absence of support from any colleague. A motion on the Urban Growth Strategy went unsupported. He was the sole vote against the Vision Lands landowner agreement that was advancing his own park concept. He was one of four against the RCMP station. One of five against the final RCMP decision. In a council of eleven where six votes are needed to accomplish anything, consistently struggling to find even one supporter is a significant constraint.

Both code of conduct violations involve the people he works with: a volunteer he disparaged and attributed false statements to, and staff he treated disrespectfully in a policy debate. The 2025 investigation's finding — that his behaviour crossed from legitimate challenge into disrespect — goes to the heart of the collaborative function. When staff feel they cannot engage with a councillor without being treated disrespectfully, oversight discussions become defensive rather than productive. When colleagues know a working session may produce a conduct complaint, the collaborative environment degrades.

After the 2021 committee incident, Bourgeois resigned from the committee rather than working through the disagreement — a pattern of exit over repair. The Vision Lands park eventually gained broad support, which shows that collaboration is possible even with Bourgeois, but it is the exception rather than the pattern.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
The public record on Bourgeois's community engagement is thin, which is itself informative. What is visible suggests he does advocate for Ward 2 interests within the council chamber — citing constituent concerns in debates, referencing what residents tell him about policing effectiveness, and responding to community concerns about crime in the west end with his 2022 public safety resolution.

He has chaired several city committees during his career — finance, social inclusion, land use planning, police services review, snow removal — which create formal touchpoints for community issues to reach the council table. His 2021 campaign explicitly positioned him as a citizen's advocate against an insular council.

The significant limitation is visibility outside the chamber. There is little documented evidence of neighbourhood events, community consultations outside formal processes, or grassroots engagement with Ward 2 residents beyond what council proceedings require. His decade-long media boycott further limits his community presence — residents who rely on CBC and other major outlets to understand their councillor's positions and reasoning cannot access Bourgeois through those channels. A councillor who does good work but refuses to communicate it through mainstream media is only partially fulfilling the representational function that democratic office requires.

Bourgeois's orchestration of this opposition sits uneasily alongside any claim to genuine community engagement. His explicit rationale — that her criticism of his own Eastgate vote demonstrated 'rigid bias' that disqualified her from advisory work — reveals a view of citizen participation that is conditional on agreement with council decisions. A councillor who positions himself as a champion of institutional accountability while leading the charge to exclude a community activist from a volunteer planning committee is not operating from consistent principles.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.note: UPDATED: Revised from A- to B+. Bourgeois is the strongest scrutiny performer on this council, but important limitations prevent an A-range grade.
categories.assessment:
Bourgeois brings genuine intellectual rigour to the oversight function that is without peer on this council. His scrutiny is not performative — it is grounded in preparation, domain knowledge, and a willingness to ask the uncomfortable questions that other councillors avoid.

When the policing authority requested additional RCMP officers for 2024, Bourgeois asked directly: was there evidence that the officers hired the previous year had made a measurable difference in outcomes? He repeatedly pressed the policing authority chair on whether any evidence base informed the hiring request. On the $57M RCMP station, his dissent was grounded in a logical sequencing argument: you should know what force you need before you build a building for it.

In committee, he consistently asks detailed questions about staff presentations — pressing on asset management methodology, urban growth assumptions, financial reporting formats, and future funding plans. His PhD in Public Policy Analysis and 27 peer-reviewed academic publications on municipalities and public institutions give him analytical tools that most councillors lack and that he demonstrably uses.

The limitations that prevent an A-range grade are real. First, his scrutiny is concentrated primarily on the policing file and fiscal questions — less visible across the full range of municipal operations including parks, recreation, transportation, and cultural services. Second, his conduct violations create a functional problem for oversight: when staff feel bullied rather than constructively challenged, oversight discussions can become defensive and information flow can degrade — ultimately undermining the accountability function he is trying to exercise. Third, some scrutiny motions go unsupported by colleagues, limiting their practical effectiveness. He is the strongest in this category on a council that often struggles to hold administration accountable — but B+ rather than A- better captures both the strength and these real constraints.

The crime reduction and prevention committee — which Bourgeois sat on alongside councillors Butler, LeBlanc, and Léger — produced a substantive report with concrete recommendations, including overhauling governance of the Codiac RCMP and empowering municipal bylaw officers as peace officers. Presenting those findings publicly, including on CBC Information Morning, reflects the kind of committee-level scrutiny work that is consistent with Bourgeois's strongest contributions this term. This is a genuine addition to the oversight record, independent of the media optics around when he chose to discuss it.

councillors.overall_assessment:
Marty Kingston is personally well-known across Moncton through his two-decade broadcasting career as the voice of the Moncton Wildcats and a regular presence at charitable and community events. That visibility is a genuine asset for a councillor-at-large — residents encounter their representative outside the formal council context, which creates a form of accessibility that most politicians cannot manufacture.

The central challenge in Kingston's assessment is the gap between his public profile and his council contribution. He campaigned on homelessness, addiction, and mental health — pressing issues in Moncton's downtown core during this term — but the public record does not document initiatives, motions, or sustained advocacy on those issues during his four years in office. The Events Moncton contribution and his principled votes on the youth group home and the Elmwood Drive subdivisions show that Kingston can make principled decisions, but they do not constitute a policy agenda.

The most documented moment of Kingston's term — his response to Bourgeois during the RCMP debate, suggesting a colleague re-read the code of conduct in response to a policy question — is not a flattering data point. It reflects a defensive instinct that escalates disagreement rather than engaging it. For a first-term, at-large councillor who nominally represents the entire city, the overall contribution falls short of what the position requires.

categories.name: Conduct & Professionalism
categories.assessment:
No formal code of conduct violations were filed against Kingston during this term, which distinguishes his record from the most serious conduct issues on this council. However, two documented incidents raise meaningful professionalism concerns.

During the February 2024 RCMP debate, when Bourgeois asked councillors who voted in favour to explain their reasoning, Kingston responded that he was "a little taken aback that we would all get asked how to explain ourselves on a yay vote" and suggested Bourgeois should "re-read the council code of conduct." Invoking the code of conduct in response to a legitimate policy question — a question about how a public official voted on a public matter — is a deflection rather than an answer, and it escalates a policy debate into a personal confrontation. Public officials in democratic bodies are expected to explain their votes, particularly on significant questions.

On the religious symbols controversy, Kingston voted in the initial closed-door session to remove the symbols, then apologized publicly at the December 4, 2023 council meeting: "I'm sincerely sorry about how the vote went" and acknowledged he "should have thought that decision through more carefully." The willingness to apologize publicly is commendable and reflects well on his character. His admission that council "didn't really get into it fully as we should have" is an honest self-assessment. But the initial failure of judgment on a matter with obvious religious and cultural sensitivity — presumably visible to any thoughtful councillor before the vote — is a genuine concern.

A planning committee appointment episode further depresses Kingston's conduct grade. He was the last councillor to add his name to the email opposition, writing that the applicant had 'often, seemingly without an understanding of how municipal governments function, criticized Council and Councillors.' The condescension is notable: the applicant is a 15-year non-profit veteran who was vetted and recommended by city staff. Characterizing her criticism as ignorance rather than legitimate disagreement — and using that characterization to justify blocking her from a volunteer advisory role — is a conduct failure. Combined with the RCMP debate deflection, a pattern emerges of treating accountability as an affront rather than a feature of democratic governance.

categories.name: Transparency & Accountability
categories.assessment:
Kingston did not champion transparency initiatives during this term. He participated in the closed-door religious symbols vote without raising process concerns until public backlash made reversal politically necessary. He voted with the majority (6-5) to keep the RCMP without public consultation, supporting a major decision that bypassed community input.

His response to Bourgeois's request for vote explanation during the RCMP debate is the most telling transparency data point: Kingston treated a request for public explanation of a public vote as an inappropriate imposition. For an elected official, explaining voting decisions is not optional — it is a core accountability function. Treating it as an unwelcome intrusion reveals a narrow view of what transparency in democratic office requires.

His voting record is publicly documented through council minutes, and he engages with constituents through social media and community events. But the standard for transparency extends well beyond having votes on record — it includes proactively communicating reasoning, supporting robust public engagement processes, and welcoming rather than resisting public scrutiny.

categories.name: Effectiveness & Initiative
categories.assessment:
Kingston served on the Events Moncton committee and contributed to the organization of the 2023 IIHF World Junior Hockey Championship, described as a "huge success" for the region. That is a concrete contribution that leverages his unique broadcasting and events background in a way no other councillor could replicate as effectively.

His voting record shows principled positions on specific issues: he voted against the Elmwood Drive subdivisions (supporting staff anti-sprawl recommendations), supported the youth group home rezoning (one of only three in favour), and supported the unanimous religious symbols reversal. These votes demonstrate a willingness to take positions on difficult issues rather than defaulting to the path of least resistance.

The fundamental gap is between campaign commitments and documented action. Kingston campaigned on homelessness, drug addiction, and mental health — the most visible crisis on Moncton's downtown streets during his entire term. The public record does not document policy motions, committee advocacy, or sustained engagement with service providers on these issues during his four years in office. The gap between stated priorities and documented action is the central concern in this category.

categories.name: Collaboration & Relationship-Building
categories.assessment:
The RCMP debate exchange with Bourgeois represents Kingston's most clearly documented collaborative failure. Responding to a policy question by suggesting a colleague re-read the code of conduct is the kind of interpersonal escalation that erodes working relationships on a council of eleven, where informal trust and communication outside formal proceedings are essential to effectiveness.

On the positive side, Kingston supported the unanimous menorah reversal, demonstrating willingness to change position when consensus shifts. He supported the youth group home alongside only two other colleagues, showing willingness to take unpopular positions. He participated in Events Moncton committee work.

However, there is limited evidence of Kingston building coalitions, bridging factions on divisive votes, or championing compromise positions on the major contested issues of the term. He appears to function primarily as a voter — casting his ballot on proposals from administration and other councillors — rather than as a policy initiator or consensus broker. For a councillor-at-large representing the entire city, that is a limited contribution.

categories.name: Community Engagement & Representation
categories.assessment:
Kingston's broadcasting career gives him a genuine community presence that most politicians cannot manufacture. As the longtime voice of the Moncton Wildcats and a regular MC at charitable events, he is personally known across the city — residents encounter him at games, galas, and community events in ways that create informal accessibility to their at-large representative.

His coaching involvement with Lewisville Minor Hockey and Moncton Lions Minor Baseball represents grassroots community engagement that connects him directly to families and youth in the city. These connections are authentic, developed over years, and not reducible to electoral strategy.

The limitation is the translation gap: Kingston's community presence is relational and social rather than policy-driven. There is limited evidence that he uses his community platform to advance specific policy positions, gather constituent input on municipal issues, or report back on council activity in structured ways. Personal visibility and policy representation are different things, and the former does not automatically produce the latter.

A planning committee appointment vote is the most concrete failure in Kingston's engagement record. His existing grade reflected limited documented engagement beyond events and broadcasting. This incident adds an active failure: participating in the exclusion of a vetted citizen from the Municipal Plan Review Committee — a major decade-long planning process — specifically because she had used her public platform to criticize council decisions. A councillor-at-large whose mandate extends across all of Moncton should be especially attentive to citizen participation in city-wide planning; that vote is the opposite of that.

categories.name: Scrutiny & Oversight
categories.assessment:
Kingston participated in budget deliberations and the multi-year policing review as part of council's standard oversight processes. He voted against the Elmwood Drive subdivisions, supporting staff anti-sprawl recommendations against a majority council decision — a form of judgment-based oversight on planning matters.
